summaries.example: Imagine you invent a new playground game. You use familiar ideas, such as running and tossing a ball, but combine them in your own way. The game is new to you, and it works well enough for others to enjoy. This shows how creativity can involve newness, usefulness, and a process that includes trying, choosing, and improving.
summaries.summary: Creativity is not only about art. People can be creative in science, mathematics, technology, writing, games, and everyday problem-solving. Philosophers ask what makes something creative. A common answer is that it must be new and valuable, but there is disagreement about both parts. A silly new idea might be original but not useful. Also, a discovery can be creative for one person even if another person found it first. Some philosophers think the way an idea is made matters too: it may need to be surprising, made independently rather than copied, partly unplanned, or produced by an agent—a being that acts. Creative work is usually not one magical flash. It can involve practice and preparation, generating possibilities, an “aha” moment, checking ideas, and making the idea into a drawing, story, design, or other product. Imagination helps because it lets us safely try combinations that are not yet real. The entry also discusses computers. A computer may produce new and useful results, but philosophers still debate whether it genuinely creates or merely follows processes designed by people.
key_ideas: Creativity can describe a person, a process, or a product such as an idea or object.
Many thinkers say a creative product must be new and valuable, but some philosophers challenge the value part.
Something can be new to its maker even if someone else discovered it long ago.
Creative work often includes learning, making ideas, noticing an insight, judging ideas, and turning ideas into something others can see or hear.
Philosophers disagree about whether computers can truly be creative or only act as if they are.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about creativity helps us understand art, inventions, discoveries, and ordinary problem-solving. It also reminds us that creative work usually takes knowledge, practice, judgment, and revision—not just sudden inspiration. These questions can help us think carefully about our own ideas and about whether a machine deserves credit for something it produces.

important_terms.definition: Making or producing something new, such as an idea, action, design, story, or invention.
Being new, at least to the person who makes or discovers something.
How well something works, helps, fits a goal, or is worthwhile. Philosophers disagree about whether creativity always needs this.
A mental ability to picture, combine, or change ideas without having to believe they are true right away.
A useful rule of thumb that guides thinking but leaves room for choices and new ideas.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be creative if it is new but does not help anyone?
Is copying always uncreative, or can learning from others lead to an original idea?
Can following a helpful rule make it easier to be creative?
Does a creative act need to be planned on purpose?

summaries.example: Suppose a student independently rediscovers a familiar philosophical position while writing an essay. The position is not historically new, but it is new to the student, so it may be psychologically creative. If the student did not copy it, used background knowledge in an unexpected way, evaluated whether the argument worked, and revised it into a coherent essay, the process displays several features philosophers associate with creativity. Whether the argument is valuable, and whether intentional agency is required, remain further questions.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of creativity asks what makes a person, process, or product creative, and it is not reducible to the philosophy of art. A widely used account says that a creative product is novel and valuable, where value may mean useful, effective, fitting, or worthwhile. Yet philosophers dispute the value condition. Examples of harmful or ineffective innovations suggest that creativity might not require goodness in an ordinary moral sense, although some theorists preserve a weaker kind of value, such as effectiveness for an intended purpose. Novelty is also qualified. Newton’s calculus could be creative for Newton even if Leibniz had arrived at it earlier; this illustrates psychological rather than historical creativity. Other accounts add process requirements. A product may need to arise through surprise, independent originality, spontaneity, or agency. These proposals connect judgments about a product to assumptions about how it was made. The entry also considers whether creativity is a virtue and whether it can be learned. One argument says that creativity is a disposition involving ability and motivation, both of which can sometimes be strengthened through practice and heuristics. Cognitive-scientific approaches describe creative work through interacting operations such as preparation, generation, insight, evaluation, and externalization. These operations need not occur in a neat sequence. Finally, AI systems can produce novel and useful outputs, but debate remains over whether this shows genuine creativity or only creative-looking behavior, especially when agency is treated as essential.
key_ideas: The philosophy of creativity is broader than aesthetics: it concerns creative persons, processes, and products across many domains.
The standard psychological definition treats creativity as involving novelty and value, but philosophical objections include cases of immoral or ineffective creativity.
Novelty need not mean new in all history. A result can be psychologically creative while lacking historical novelty.
Several proposed process conditions—surprise, originality, spontaneity, and agency—attempt to explain what makes the production of a new product creative.
Creativity may be learnable because practice, motivation, skills, imagination, and heuristics can improve a person’s disposition to produce new things.

Cognitive science studies creativity as a natural, multi-operation process, while artificial-intelligence research raises separate questions about merely appearing creative and genuinely being creative.
summaries.why_it_matters: The concept of creativity affects how we understand artistic achievement, scientific discovery, education, invention, and artificial intelligence. Examining its conditions prevents overly simple pictures: creativity may require both freedom and discipline, imagination and evaluation, individual originality and learned skill. The debates also show how judgments about products can depend on hidden assumptions about processes, intentions, responsibility, and the kinds of beings that can create.

important_terms.definition: A person, process, or product counts as creative under an account that typically requires novelty and, often, value.
Newness relative to the creator or to all of human history. Psychological novelty is new to the creator; historical novelty is new in history.
The usefulness, effectiveness, appropriateness, or other worth of a product; philosophers disagree about whether it is necessary for creativity.
The independent production of an idea rather than copying it, even when another person has already produced a similar idea.
The feature of a process in which its exact result is not fully planned or controlled in advance.
The capacity of a creator to act through choice, judgment, understanding, and possibly intention.
A structured system of elements and constraints that defines possible ways of thinking or making within a domain.
A loose rule of thumb that guides inquiry without mechanically fixing the result.

questions_to_think_about: Does calling something creative necessarily praise it, or can immoral and ineffective products still be creative?
Is independent discovery enough for originality, or must the process contain some further kind of innovation?
Can a carefully trained person be creative while following heuristics?
If a system produces surprising and useful results, what additional reason would be needed to call it an agent?
Does a scientific explanation of creativity need to predict a result exactly, or can it explain only contributing processes and conditions?

summaries.example: A student is designing a phone app to help classmates organize homework. She combines a calendar with a game-like point system, tests several versions, rejects features that confuse users, and revises the design. The app may be creative because it is new to her and useful for a task. But if she copied the whole idea without understanding it, some philosophers would say the product lacks originality even if it is new in her classroom.
summaries.summary: Creativity raises philosophical questions that apply far beyond paintings and music. A person, a process, or a product can be called creative, and products include ideas, performances, inventions, and solutions. The most common definition says that creativity requires novelty plus value. Novelty is widely accepted, but it is usually understood relative to the creator: an idea can be creative for a student even if philosophers or scientists proposed it earlier. Value is more controversial. Some theorists think a creative thing must be useful, effective, or worthwhile. Others point to harmful or unsuccessful designs and argue that creativity may not require value, or may require only effectiveness for a chosen purpose. Further proposals focus on the process. Creativity might involve surprise, originality in the sense of not copying, spontaneity, or agency. Agency means that an actor’s choices and judgments help produce the result. These conditions lead to disagreements about natural patterns and computer outputs. The entry also rejects the idea that creativity must be pure inspiration. Creative work can involve preparation, practice, generating and combining ideas, insight, evaluation, and expressing an idea in a concrete form. Flexible heuristics can teach people how to approach problems without giving them a fixed answer. Psychology and neuroscience investigate these processes, while AI research asks whether systems that make new and useful things are genuinely creative or only imitate creativity.
key_ideas: Creativity may belong to a creator, a creative process, or a creative product such as an idea, performance, or artifact.
The common view that creativity requires novelty and value is influential but contested.
Philosophers distinguish being new to a person from being new in all of history.
Some accounts require more than a new product: the process may need to be surprising, independent, spontaneous, or agent-produced.
Creative thinking can involve imagination, unconscious incubation, practice, evaluation, and externalizing ideas through sketches or other forms.
Research on computers asks whether producing creative-looking outputs is enough, or whether genuine creativity requires agency and responsibility.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding creativity matters because people use it to solve problems, communicate, invent, and make meaning. It also matters in education: learning techniques and practicing skills need not destroy originality. Philosophical analysis helps us separate several questions that are often mixed together—whether something is new, whether it is valuable, how it was produced, and who or what should receive credit for it.

important_terms.definition: The ability or activity of producing something new, often with usefulness or other value, in art, science, technology, or daily life.
Newness. It can mean new to the creator, called psychological novelty, or new to everyone in history, called historical novelty.
The quality of being useful, effective, fitting, or worthwhile. Philosophers disagree about whether this must be part of creativity.
Producing something independently rather than simply copying another person’s result.
Happening without a complete plan or exact prediction of the final result.
The involvement of a chooser or actor in producing a result, possibly through intention and judgment.
A system of ideas and rules that sets the possibilities within a field, such as chess, grammar, or music.
A flexible strategy or rule of thumb that helps solve problems without determining one exact answer.

questions_to_think_about: Would a harmful invention still count as creative if it was carefully designed and original?
Why might discovering an old idea independently be creative?
How can rules or practice support creativity instead of limiting it?
Is an accidental pattern made by wind or by a person creative? Why might agency matter?
Should a computer receive credit for an output that its programmers did not predict?
